why: One step of a cellular state machine: walk the eight neighbours with a direction-offset table, and compute every new state from the ORIGINAL grid, so updates must go into a separate grid (or be encoded so the old value survives).
hints: Why can't you overwrite cells as you go?
Each cell's next state depends on neighbours' current states. Count neighbours with a list of the eight (dr, dc) offsets, skipping those outside the grid.
Fill a fresh grid: live stays live with 2 or 3 neighbours, dead becomes live with exactly 3. O(rows * cols * 8). (In-place: encode old and new in two bits.)
pitfalls: Updating in place without encoding makes later cells see already-updated neighbours.
Do not count the cell itself among its neighbours.
Edge and corner cells have fewer neighbours; bounds-check every offset.
